summary: This informational RFC is an index summarizing the RFCs numbered 2000 through 2099, as part of a long-running series of summary documents. It helps readers find what was published in that range.

plainLanguage.summary: A table of contents for a hundred notes the Internet community wrote.

questions: how to find an rfc by date
subtitle: An index of the 100 RFCs published in 1996-1997.

tldr.problem: The RFC series had grown to hundreds of documents, and readers needed a way to find what was published in a particular time period.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2099 is a summaries of all 100 RFCs from 2000 through 2099, listing each by number, title, author, date and a brief description.
tldr.outcome: These periodic summaries help the Internet community track the large volume of published standards and informational documents, though the practice was eventually discontinued.

today: RFC 2099 is an informational document that has not been obsoleted, so it remains a valid historical summary of RFCs 2000-2099. The practice of publishing regular summary RFCs was eventually discontinued as online search became widely available.

sections.title: What This Document Does
sections.content:
RFC 2099 is an informational summary document that lists all Request for Comments numbered from 2000 through 2099. The RFC series publishes standards, experimental protocols and informational notes on Internet technologies. As the number of RFCs had grown very large by the 1990s, periodic summaries like this one helped readers understand what had been published recently.

Each RFC in the list appears with its number, the author's name, the publication date, the title, and one or two sentences describing what it covers. The document notes which RFCs were on the standards track and which were experimental, helping readers quickly identify the status of work in particular areas.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine your library publishes a hundred new books a year. This document is like a card catalog that lists them all in order, so you can find one about the topic you care about without reading all hundred.

sections.title: A Sample of the Coverage
sections.content:
The 100 RFCs in this summary span a wide range of Internet technologies published in late 1996 and early 1997. They include protocols for email (IMAP4, MIME, SMTP extensions), the World Wide Web (HTTP/1.1 and Digest authentication), network management (MIB modules, SNMP extensions), security (DNS security, authentication mechanisms), routing (RIPng, Mobile IP), and multimedia (RTP payload formats for video and audio).

Some of the summaries note RFCs that update or obsolete earlier work. For instance, RFC 2060 (IMAP4rev1) is a newer version of the IMAP protocol, and RFC 2001 documents TCP algorithms that had never been formally specified before. The summaries help readers see how the standards have evolved and which RFCs to consult depending on their implementation date.
sections.plainLanguage: These hundred documents cover everything from sending email safely to video conferences to how routers find the best path for messages. Each one solves one part of the Internet puzzle.

sections.title: Standards Track and Experimental Work
sections.content:
The document notes which RFCs are on the standards track, meaning they are working toward becoming official Internet Standards. Many others are marked experimental, meaning they describe techniques still being researched or tried but not yet proven in wide deployment. A few are informational only, providing useful background or describing something that happened in the Internet community but not defining a protocol.

This classification helps implementors understand the maturity and stability of each RFC. Standards-track documents have gone through formal review; experimental ones may change. The document advises readers to check the latest Internet Official Protocol Standards document for current status, since the standards process moves work between stages over time.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of these documents say 'this is how we officially do it now,' while others say 'we're trying this as an experiment' or 'this is just interesting background.' The marker tells you how much you can rely on it.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
Summary documents like RFC 2099 were valuable snapshots of what the Internet community was working on during a specific time window. By grouping 100 RFCs at a time, they made it possible for researchers, administrators and engineers to skim a single document and understand the landscape of recent work without having to read 100 separate RFCs or search a full database.

The RFC series itself has no built-in way to search or browse by topic or date; it is simply numbered in publication order. Periodic summaries filled that gap for readers of their era. While modern tools and search engines have made these summaries less necessary today, they remain a historical record of what the Internet standards community considered important in each period.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the web made it easy to search for things, a document like this was really handy. You could pick it up, glance through it, and say 'oh, they made a new video protocol' or 'here's how mobile phones should connect to the Internet' without searching everywhere.
